chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Statistical Toolkit for Spotting Reversion

lessons.title: Case Study: Calculating Z-Score and Half-Life for an NSE Stock in Python

children.text: Three lessons, three tools: z-score to measure how stretched a price is, phi and half-life to measure how fast it typically snaps back, and theta to express that same speed independent of how often you sample the data. A real analysis does not use these one at a time. It runs all of them together, on one stock, to answer a single practical question: is this specific deviation, right now, actually worth trading? This case study builds that full pipeline end to end in Python.

body.text: A usable mean reversion signal needs two things to line up at once: the price must be statistically stretched right now (a large z-score), and the stock must have a track record of correcting that kind of stretch quickly (a short half-life). Either one on its own is a weak, incomplete signal.

children.text: The Data: A Hypothetical NSE Midcap, 90 Trading Days

Take a hypothetical NSE-listed midcap, call it Beta Chemicals, with 90 trading days of daily closing prices loaded into a pandas Series, pulled from a broker API like Zerodha's Kite Connect or any historical NSE data source. Over its most recent stretch, the stock has been sliding, and the question is whether that slide is a tradeable overreaction or something to leave alone.

body.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# 'close' is a pandas Series of Beta Chemicals' last 90 daily closes
window = 20
rolling_mean = close.rolling(window).mean()
rolling_std = close.rolling(window).std()
z_score = (close - rolling_mean) / rolling_std

deviation = (close - rolling_mean).dropna()
x = deviation.shift(1).dropna()
y = deviation.loc[x.index]
phi = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0]

theta = -np.log(phi)
half_life = np.log(2) / theta

print(f"Latest close: {close.iloc[-1]:.2f}")
print(f"Latest z-score: {z_score.iloc[-1]:.2f}")
print(f"Estimated phi: {phi:.3f}")
print(f"Half-life: {half_life:.1f} trading days")

children.text: Neither number alone would be enough. A z-score of -2.18 with no information about speed could belong to a stock that takes three months to correct, by which point holding costs, opportunity cost, and the odds of something else happening to the business all pile up. A half-life of 2.8 days on its own, with no information about current stretch, just describes a stock's general personality, it says nothing about whether today is actually a good day to trade it. Put together, they answer the real question: right now, is this stock both far enough from home and quick enough to get back for the trade to be worth the risk?

body.caption: A simple decision matrix: combining stretch and speed

cells: Strong candidate: statistically stretched and historically quick to correct
Caution: stretched, but slow, closer to a random walk, or possibly a structural break (Chapter 8)
Nothing to trade yet: a fast reverter, but no current deviation worth acting on
Avoid: neither currently stretched nor historically reliable at correcting

body.text: Landing in the "strong candidate" box is necessary, not sufficient. Chapter 1 already showed that a large deviation can reflect a genuine, permanent change rather than an overreaction. Before sizing a real trade on Beta Chemicals' numbers, you would still need to check for exactly that: results due, promoter pledge activity, sector-wide news, anything that would explain the fall as something other than statistical noise around an intact business. This pipeline tells you where to look. It does not replace looking.

children.text: Scaling Up: Screening Many Stocks at Once
Wrap the same logic in a function and you can run it across an entire watchlist in one pass, keeping only the names that clear both bars at once.

body.code:
import numpy as np

def zscore_and_halflife(close, window=20):
    rolling_mean = close.rolling(window).mean()
    rolling_std = close.rolling(window).std()
    z = (close - rolling_mean) / rolling_std

    deviation = (close - rolling_mean).dropna()
    x = deviation.shift(1).dropna()
    y = deviation.loc[x.index]
    phi = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0]
    half_life = -np.log(2) / np.log(phi) if 0 < phi < 1 else np.nan

    return z.iloc[-1], half_life

# 'universe' is a dict of {ticker: pandas Series of daily closes}
candidates = []
for ticker, close in universe.items():
    z, hl = zscore_and_halflife(close)
    if abs(z) > 2 and hl < 10:
        candidates.append((ticker, round(z, 2), round(hl, 1)))

print(sorted(candidates, key=lambda c: abs(c[1]), reverse=True))
body.caption: A basic screener: keep only tickers with a statistically stretched z-score and a half-life under 10 trading days.

body.text: This loop is a rough sketch of the reversion watchlist Chapter 8 builds properly at the end of this course, once you also have the failure checks from Chapters 1 and 8 folded in as additional filters, not just the statistics.

body.title: Compute Gamma Textiles' z-score
body.prompt: Gamma Textiles is trading at ₹379. Its 20-day rolling mean is ₹340 and its 20-day rolling standard deviation is ₹14. What is its current z-score, rounded to two decimal places?
body.explanation: (379 - 340) / 14 = 39 / 14 = 2.79. Gamma Textiles is trading unusually far above its own recent average, a candidate worth checking for half-life next, exactly the next step in the pipeline this lesson built.

body.title: Which stock is the strongest combined candidate?
body.question: Four stocks show the following current z-score and half-life. Which is the strongest mean reversion candidate right now?
body.explanation: Stock C has both a large current deviation (|z| = 2.9, comfortably past the common ±2 threshold) and a short half-life (4 days, well within the tradeable range from Lesson 6). Stock A is fast-reverting but not currently stretched. Stock B is stretched but slow, closer to a random walk than a reliable reverter. Stock D is neither stretched nor fast. Only Stock C lands in the "strong candidate" box of the decision matrix.

points: A usable mean reversion signal combines two dimensions at once: current stretch (z-score) and historical reversion speed (half-life). Either alone is a weak, incomplete signal.
A large z-score with a long half-life is a caution, not a green light, it may reflect a slow-moving or structurally broken series rather than a tradeable overreaction.
The same z-score and half-life pipeline can be wrapped in a function and run across an entire watchlist to screen for candidates that clear both bars at once.

Clearing both statistical bars is necessary, not sufficient. Chapters 1 and 8's fundamental checks still have to confirm the deviation is a genuine overreaction, not a structural break, before real capital goes into the trade.

This closes the statistical toolkit chapter. Chapter 3 puts it to work building the actual single-asset trading strategies, Bollinger Bands, RSI, and moving-average reversion, that these tools support.
